passage:
In the engineering hostel, Imran had stopped going to the mess for breakfast. Most mornings he lay on the top bunk, scrolling, feeling flat and heavy while assignments piled up. At noon Himani from the next wing found him in the common room. "Walk to the tea stall with me? Ten minutes, that's all."
He went, grumbling. The sun on the path felt oddly nice. Back in his room, he finished half a problem set.
The next morning he planned a big fix: gym at six, a long run daily, no excuses. He managed one day, then slept through the alarm and felt worse than before.
Himani shook her head. "Forget the gym plan. Just the tea stall walk. Every day, even on bad days. And if the flatness hangs on, the campus counsellor is there too."
So that's what he does. It doesn't fix everything, but most days his head feels a little clearer afterwards.

qa.a: A short daily walk is easier to keep as a gentle habit than an all-or-nothing plan that ends in failure.

qa.a: Himani likely feels quietly pleased, seeing that the small walk helps Imran more than the big plan did.

grounding: A young adult feeling flat finds that a short daily walk lifts energy and thinking a little, as a gentle habit rather than an all-or-nothing plan.

passage:
Dear Maria,
Since you asked how I've been since the placement rejections: flat, mostly. For a few weeks I barely left my room. Then my roommate dragged me out for a walk along the Kochi seafront, and I noticed my head felt a bit less foggy afterwards.
So I've kept it up. Twenty minutes every evening, no targets, no tracking. At first I turned it into a punishment: walk faster, you lazy idiot. That made me hate it. Now I walk slowly on bad days and let that count too. Some days it's just to the ferry and back.
It hasn't turned my life around. But I'm sleeping better, and I've started applying again. Small and regular seems to beat big and occasional.
Write soon,
Divyansh

qa.a: Divyansh walks along the Kochi seafront.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about the walks when they were a punishment?
qa.a: Divyansh felt resentful and discouraged, hating walks that had become a punishment full of insults like "lazy idiot".

qa.q: What change made the walking habit last?
qa.a: Dropping targets, walking slowly on bad days and letting that count, so the habit stayed gentle and regular.

qa.q: How might Maria feel reading that Divyansh has started applying again?
qa.a: Maria would likely feel relieved and hopeful, having asked how things were after the rejections.

grounding: A young adult in a low patch finds a short daily walk lifts energy a little once it becomes a gentle habit instead of a punishment.
